1.open: Think of a time you were in the dark, like a power cut or a camping trip. What did you notice when the light finally came back on?
questions: The writer says, "which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands" (v. 1). Why might it matter that Jesus was a real person people could see and touch, and not only an idea?
Verse 3 says, "We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us." What does fellowship look like in your own life, and where is it hard to find?
Verse 5 says, "God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all." What does light make you think of when you picture God, and does that picture feel comforting, uncomfortable, or both?

Verse 6 says that if we claim to be close to God "yet walk in the darkness, we lie." What do you think it looks like to say one thing and live another? Where do people in general, or you in particular, slip into that?
Verse 7 says, "if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another." Why might honesty with God and honesty with each other go together?
Verse 8 says, "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves." Why is it so easy to explain away our own wrongs? What helps you see them more honestly?
Verse 9 says, "He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." If you are honest, what comes up in you when you hear that? Is it relief, doubt, or something else?

The writer says in verse 7 that Jesus' blood "cleanses us from all sin." Christians read this in different ways, some as ongoing cleansing for people who will always struggle, others as allowing real freedom from deliberate sin in this life. How does each reading shape the way you think about growing as a Christian?
1.life: This week, find one quiet moment each day to tell God plainly about one thing you got wrong, using verse 9 as your guide. If there is a person you owe an honest word to, consider taking one step toward saying it.
1.prayer: Thank God that he is light and that he is "faithful and just to forgive." Ask for the courage to be honest about your failures, and for a group where people can be real with each other.
1.tip: Verses 8 to 10 can make people feel judged or can stir up old guilt. Keep returning to verse 9, which is about God's faithfulness, not our performance. Also, do not push anyone to confess anything out loud in the group. Let people share only what they choose, and let the leader go first with something small and honest.

2.open: Think of someone whose actions have always matched their words. What did you notice about them?
questions: John writes so that his readers "will not sin," and then adds that if anyone does sin, "we have an advocate before the Father" (vv. 1-2). How does it feel to hear both of those things in the same breath?
Verse 2 calls Jesus "the atoning sacrifice for our sins." In your own words, what do you think that means, and why might it matter on a day you feel you have let God down?
John says, "Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked" (v. 6). What is one way you have seen Jesus' way of living make a difference in an ordinary situation?
John calls the command to love an old one and also a new one (vv. 7-8). Why might something familiar feel fresh again when you see someone actually live it out?
Verse 11 says the person who hates a fellow believer "does not know where he is going." Have you ever carried a grudge and noticed it affecting more than just that relationship?
In verse 16 John lists "the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life." Which of these tends to tug at you most, and what does it look like in your daily routine?
John says those who left "did not belong to us" (v. 19). That can sound harsh, especially if someone you love has walked away from faith. How might you hold this verse with care?
If you are honest, where do you find it hard to be sure that you truly know God? What helps you, or what would help you, in that place?
2.life: Pick one relationship where there is distance or a grudge. This week, do one small, concrete act of love toward that person, such as a message, a meal or a kind word, and ask God to help you walk as Jesus walked.
2.prayer: Thank Jesus for speaking for us when we fail. Ask God to help your life match what you say you believe, and to soften any place where you are holding on to hurt.
2.tip: Verses 3 to 6 can sound like a test that sets people up to fail, and anxious members may hear it that way. Remind the group that John opens with forgiveness (vv. 1-2) and that he is describing the direction of a life, not perfection. Also, Christians differ over whether verse 2 means Jesus died to actually save every person or only those who come to believe, so name that briefly and keep the focus on the comfort of the verse.

3.open: Who is someone who showed up for you in a practical way when you needed help, and what did they do?
questions: John begins with wonder: "Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God" (v. 1). What does it mean to you to be called a child of God, and is it easy or hard to believe?
John says "what we will be has not yet been revealed," but "when Christ appears, we will be like Him" (v. 2). How does hope about the future change the way you live today?

Verses 6 to 9 sound strict: "No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning" (v. 6). Christians read this differently, and most take it as a settled pattern of life, not perfection. How do these verses land with you, and where do you feel afraid or unsure reading them?
John says Christ "appeared to take away sins" (v. 5) and "to destroy the works of the devil" (v. 8). What does it look like when someone is being freed from sin rather than just trying harder?

John points to Cain as the opposite of love (v. 12), and says hating a brother is like murder (v. 15). Why might John treat cold or bitter feelings so seriously? Where do you see that kind of hatred show up in small ways?

Verse 16 says "Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers." Most of us will never face that exact choice. What might laying down your life look like on an ordinary Tuesday?

Verse 17 asks how God's love can abide in someone who sees a brother in need and "withholds his compassion." When has someone's practical help meant more to you than their words? When have you held back, and why?

Verse 20 says, "Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things." When does your conscience accuse you, and what would it mean to bring that to a God who is greater than it?
3.life: John says, "let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth" (v. 18). This week, pick one person with a real need, such as a meal, a ride, a call or some money, and meet it in a practical way.
3.prayer: Thank God for calling us his children. Ask him to quiet a heart that condemns you, and to show you one person you can love with action this week.
3.tip: Verses 6 to 9 can leave sincere people anxious about whether they are really saved. Say plainly that most readers see a settled direction of life here, not sinless perfection, that some traditions hold that freedom from deliberate sin is possible, and then point the group to verses 19 to 20 as the comfort John gives.

4.open: Who is someone who made you feel truly welcome the first time you met them, and what did they do?
questions: John says, "do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits" (v. 1). Where do you hear voices today that claim to speak for God, and how do you decide which ones to trust?
John's test is whether a teacher confesses that Jesus "has come in the flesh" (v. 2). Why might it matter so much that Jesus was a real human being and not just someone who seemed human?
In verse 4 John says, "greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world." What would it look like to take courage from that without turning it into pride?
Verse 8 says, "God is love." How does that line fit or clash with the picture of God you grew up with?
Verse 10 says, "not that we loved God, but that He loved us." How is a love that starts with God different from a love we have to earn? Where do you find it hard to believe that?
Christians read the phrase "atoning sacrifice for our sins" (v. 10) in different ways. Whichever way you lean, what does it tell you about how far God was willing to go for us?

Verse 18 says, "perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment." What fears about God, or about being good enough, still follow you around? You can answer honestly, even if the verse feels hard to believe right now.
John says anyone who claims to love God but "hates his brother" is "a liar" (v. 20). Who is one person that is hard for you to love, and what might a small, real step toward them look like?
4.life: Pick one person who is hard for you to love. This week, do one specific, quiet thing for them, like a text, a prayer by name, or a favor, and remember verse 19: "We love because He first loved us."
4.prayer: Thank God that he loved us first, before we did anything to earn it. Ask him to calm the fears that keep you from trusting his love, and to help you love one real person this week.
4.tip: Verses 20 and 21 can leave people feeling guilty about someone they struggle to love, and verse 18 can sting if someone lives with fear or anxiety. Remind the group that John is pointing to God's love first, and that growing in love is a journey, not a test they have already failed.

5.open: What is something you were completely sure about as a kid that turned out not to be true?
questions: John says "everyone born of God overcomes the world" and that "this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith" (v. 4). What does the world pull you toward most, and what does it look like for faith to hold up against that?
Verse 3 says "His commandments are not burdensome." Is that how obedience feels to you lately? What makes it feel heavy or light?

In verses 6 to 8 John points to "the Spirit, the water, and the blood." Most readers take the water as Jesus' baptism and the blood as his death, though Christians read these words in more than one way. Why might it matter to John that Jesus really lived and really died?
John says "the testimony of God is greater" than human testimony (v. 9). Whose word do you trust most when something important is at stake, and why?
Verse 12 says, "Whoever has the Son has life." In your own words, what does it mean to have life in Jesus, and how is that different from just following rules?
John writes "so that you may know that you have eternal life" (v. 13). Do you feel sure of that most days, or does doubt creep in? Be as honest as you like. What helps you, or what gets in the way?
Verse 14 promises that "if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us." What do you make of that? Tell about a prayer that was hard to understand or still has no answer.
The letter ends with "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (v. 21). What are some modern idols, things that quietly take the place of God without looking like a statue?
5.life: John wants his readers to know, not just hope. This week, write down two or three things that give you reason to trust Jesus, and read them over whenever doubt shows up. If you are not sure what to write, tell God that honestly and ask for help.
5.prayer: Thank God for giving life in his Son. Ask him to make you sure of his love where you doubt, and to loosen your grip on anything that has taken his place.
5.tip: Verses 16 and 17 mention a "sin that leads to death" without explaining it, and scholars are unsure what John means. Some people may worry they have done something unforgivable. Say plainly that the passage is unclear, point back to verse 13 where John writes so that believers may know they have life, and offer to talk privately with anyone who is troubled.
